title: Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs I
notes:
## Intuition

Choosing `arr1` also fixes `arr2` (`arr2[i] = nums[i] - arr1[i]`), so it is enough to count valid `arr1` arrays. Trying them all is exponential, but whether index `i` may hold a value depends only on the value at `i - 1`. That makes (index, value of `arr1`) a natural two-dimensional DP state.

Moving from `prev` at `i - 1` to `value` at `i` needs `prev <= value` (so `arr1` does not drop) and `nums[i - 1] - prev >= nums[i] - value` (so `arr2` does not grow). Both together say `prev <= value - rise` with `rise = max(0, nums[i] - nums[i - 1])`. Every cell is therefore the sum of a prefix of the previous row, and a running total delivers each one in O(1).

## Approach

1. Let `dp[i][value]` count the valid ways to fill indices `0..i` with `arr1[i] = value`. In row 0, every `value` from 0 to `nums[0]` has exactly one way.
2. For each later index `i`, compute `rise`, the least amount `arr1` must grow there.
3. Sweep `value` upward from 0 to `nums[i]`. Once `value - rise` is a real index, add `dp[i - 1][value - rise]` to `running`; store `running` as `dp[i][value]`.
4. Sum the last row modulo `10^9 + 7`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 3, 2]`, so row 0 is `[1, 1, 1]` for values 0 to 2.

- `i = 1`: `rise = 1`. Value 0 has no predecessor; values 1, 2 and 3 pick up running totals 1, 2 and 3, giving `[0, 1, 2, 3]`.
- `i = 2`: `rise = 0`. Running totals of row 1 give `[0, 1, 3]` for values 0 to 2.

The last row sums to `0 + 1 + 3 = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · m), with m = max(nums) ≤ 50: each cell is filled once in constant time.
- Space: O(n · m) for the table; keeping only the previous row would cut it to O(m).

## Pitfalls

- Checking only `prev <= value` ignores `arr2` and overcounts; the bound is `value - rise`.
- `value - rise` is negative for small values: those cells stay 0.
- Reduce `running` and `total` modulo `10^9 + 7` as you go; the raw counts pass 2^53 quickly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `top` | largest value in `nums`, so rows have `top + 1` cells |
| `dp[i][value]` | ways to fill indices `0..i` with `arr1[i] = value` |
| `rise` | least growth of `arr1` from `i - 1` to `i` |
| `running` | sum of `dp[i - 1][0..value - rise]` |
| `total` | sum of the last row, the answer |

narration.2: Counts grow very fast, so every sum is reduced modulo 10^9 + 7.
narration.4: No part can exceed the largest value in nums, so that sets the width of each row.
narration.5: dp[i][value] will count the valid ways to fill indices 0..i with arr1[i] equal to value.
narration.6: At index 0 the first part may be anything from 0 to nums[0].
narration.7: Each such choice is one valid start, since nothing comes before it.
narration.9: Build the rows one index at a time from the previous row.
narration.10: If nums goes up here, arr2 can only avoid growing if arr1 grows at least that much, so rise is arr1's minimum step.
narration.11: running will hold the sum of dp[i - 1][0..value - rise] as value increases.
narration.12: Try every first part at index i that keeps the second part non-negative.
narration.13: A predecessor exists only once value - rise is a real index.
narration.14: Exactly one more earlier value becomes allowed, so add its count to the running sum.
narration.16: All earlier values up to value - rise lead here, and running already totals them.
narration.19: Every value in the last row ends some valid pair of arrays.
narration.21: Add up the last row, keeping the total reduced.
narration.23: Return the number of monotonic pairs modulo 10^9 + 7.
